name: Login Armor
author: wpformation

sections.description:
Eight security layers. One lightweight plugin. Zero compromise.

Login Armor is a complete WordPress security stack built for agencies, freelancers and pros who deliver audit-ready sites. No premium tier, no bundled marketing dashboard, no telemetry. Every module runs locally, ships with safe defaults, and stays out of your way.

Stop juggling Wordfence’s bloat, Solid Security’s upsells, and Limit Login Attempts’ gaps. Login Armor delivers eight independent modules in under one megabyte, with the discipline of an enterprise plugin and the licensing of free software.

Why Login Armor

  • No upsells, ever. No “premium” tier, no “Pro” buttons greyed out in your admin. Every feature is GPL.
  • No external services to sign up for. No API keys, no remote dashboards, no third-party telemetry. Two optional integrations (Have I Been Pwned for breach detection, Slack/Discord/webhook for notifications) only fire when you explicitly enable them.
  • Built to be invisible. Sub-megabyte ZIP, lazy-loaded modules, indexed queries. The plugin’s footprint stays under 2 ms on a normal login flow.
  • Multisite-aware, PHP 8.1-native. Network-activate on a fleet, configure per-site, manage from the shell with a complete WP-CLI command suite.
  • Production-grade defaults. Every toggle ships with the value an experienced admin would pick anyway. Zero-config gets you 80 percent of the protection.

Eight independent modules

1. Hide Login – Replace wp-login.php with a custom slug. Anyone hitting the old URL gets a 404 from your theme – no leakage that WordPress is even installed. Compatible with multisite, password-protected posts, reverse proxies, and password recovery flows. The branded pre-activation modal lets you pick or generate the slug before flipping the switch, and emails it to you so you can’t lock yourself out.

2. Brute Force Protection – Cascading lockouts after repeated failed logins. Locked attackers see a branded 429 landing page with a live countdown. Repeated lockouts escalate to a 24-hour ban. Lostpassword, register, XML-RPC and the REST users endpoint are all gated when an IP is locked, so attackers can’t pivot. Subnet blocking handles distributed attacks. Trusted X-Forwarded-For for sites behind Cloudflare or a load balancer.

3. Hardening – Thirteen one-click toggles across surface reduction, credential hardening, and request filtering. Disable XML-RPC, the theme/plugin file editor, the WordPress version exposure (including ?ver= on assets, even for WP 6.5+ ES modules), application passwords, author enumeration, and more. Block reserved usernames with Unicode-confusable detection. Add an invisible login honeypot. Block PHP execution in uploads and directory listing via atomic-write .htaccess rules.

4. Two-Factor Authentication – Enterprise-grade 2FA in three flavours: TOTP via any authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden), one-time codes by email, and printable backup codes. Trusted devices remembered for thirty days so you only verify once per browser. A recovery flow lets a user reset their second factor by email when the authenticator is lost, without a support ticket. Per-role enforcement, configurable grace period, and a session-aware logout.

5. Detection and Incidents – A real-time detection engine groups raw events into six attack patterns: brute force, credential stuffing, distributed scan, post-compromise activity, lockout cascade, and protocol abuse. Each incident has a drill-down view with timeline, source IPs, target users, severity, user-agent fingerprint, and one-click resolution actions (reset password, block subnet, mark resolved).

6. Activity Log – Compliance-ready audit trail of admin actions: plugin installs, settings changes, role updates, user creation, content publishing, theme switches, 2FA enrollment events. Filter, search and export to CSV with configurable retention. Seven logger domains, all togglable independently.

7. Login Page Security Headers – Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy and X-Content-Type-Options on wp-login.php and the lockout page. Two presets (standard and strict) with an optional CSP report-uri.

8. Breach Check – Detect users logging in with a password that appears in public data breach corpora, using privacy-preserving k-anonymity lookups against Have I Been Pwned. Only the first 5 hex characters of a SHA-1 prefix leave the server, the password and full hash never travel. Optional opt-in email lookup against XposedOrNot. Fail-soft: a HIBP outage never blocks login.

Plus

  • Notifications by email, Slack, Discord, or generic webhook with built-in SSRF-safe URL validation, severity threshold and rate limiting.
  • WP-CLI command suite – wp login-armor reset-slug, unblock, whitelist, incidents resolve, purge-logs, 2fa reset, 2fa devices, hardening blacklist. Full scripted operations and emergency recovery from the shell.
  • Dashboard widget – at-a-glance protection status from any admin page, with a 14-day sparkline and the six headline metrics.

Built by

Login Armor is built and maintained by WPFormation, a French WordPress agency obsessed with sites that are clean, fast, and audit-ready. We use this plugin on every site we ship.

  • Plugin overview and roadmap
  • WordPress security guides on WPFormation

GPL forever. PHP 8.1+. WordPress 6.8+. Zero dependencies.

Huit couches de securite. Un seul plugin leger. Zero compromis.

Login Armor est une stack complete de securite WordPress concue pour les agences, les freelances et les pros qui livrent des sites prets a passer un audit. Pas de version premium, pas de tableau de bord marketing integre, pas de telemetrie. Chaque module tourne en local, embarque des reglages par defaut securises, et reste discret.

Fini de jongler entre la lourdeur de Wordfence, les fenetres d’upsell de Solid Security et les angles morts de Limit Login Attempts. Login Armor regroupe huit modules independants en moins d’un mega-octet, avec la rigueur d’un plugin entreprise et la licence d’un logiciel libre.

Pourquoi Login Armor

  • Aucun upsell, jamais. Pas de niveau “premium”, pas de boutons “Pro” grises dans votre admin. Tout est en GPL.
  • Aucun service externe a activer. Pas de cle API, pas de tableau distant, pas de telemetrie tierce. Les deux integrations optionnelles (Have I Been Pwned pour la detection de fuites, Slack ou Discord ou webhook pour les notifications) ne se declenchent que si vous les activez explicitement.
  • Concu pour etre invisible. ZIP de moins d’un mega, modules charges a la demande, requetes indexees. L’empreinte sur un flux de connexion normal reste sous 2 ms.
  • Compatible multisite, natif PHP 8.1. Activation reseau possible sur une flotte, configuration par site, pilotage depuis la ligne de commande via une suite WP-CLI complete.
  • Reglages par defaut prets pour la production. Chaque bascule arrive avec la valeur qu’un admin experimente choisirait. Sans configuration, vous avez deja 80 % de la protection.

Huit modules independants

1. Masquer la connexion : remplace wp-login.php par une URL personnalisee. Toute tentative sur l’ancienne URL renvoie une 404 du theme, sans reveler la presence de WordPress. Compatible multisite, articles proteges par mot de passe, reverse proxies, et flux de recuperation de mot de passe. La modale de pre-activation vous laisse choisir ou generer le slug avant d’activer le module, et vous l’envoie par e-mail pour eviter tout verrouillage.

2. Protection contre la force brute : verrouillages en cascade apres plusieurs echecs. Les attaquants verrouilles voient une page 429 brandee avec un compte a rebours en direct. Les verrouillages repetes montent a un bannissement de 24 h. Les pages lostpassword, register, XML-RPC et l’endpoint REST users sont egalement bloques pour les IPs verrouillees, pour empecher le pivot. Blocage de sous-reseaux pour les attaques distribuees. Support de X-Forwarded-For pour les sites derriere Cloudflare ou un load balancer.

3. Renforcement : treize bascules en un clic, regroupees en reduction de surface, durcissement des identifiants et filtrage des requetes. Desactivation de XML-RPC, de l’editeur de fichiers theme/extension, de l’exposition de la version WordPress (y compris le ?ver= sur les assets, meme les modules ES de WP 6.5+), des mots de passe applicatifs, de l’enumeration des auteurs. Blocage des identifiants reserves avec detection des homoglyphes Unicode. Pot de miel invisible sur le formulaire de connexion. Blocage de l’execution PHP dans wp-content/uploads/ et desactivation du listing de repertoires via des regles .htaccess ecrites en mode atomique.

4. Authentification a deux facteurs : 2FA prete pour la production avec trois methodes : TOTP via n’importe quelle application authenticator (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden), codes a usage unique par e-mail, codes de secours imprimables. Appareils de confiance memorises pendant trente jours, vous ne validez qu’une fois par navigateur. Une procedure de recuperation laisse l’utilisateur reinitialiser son second facteur par e-mail en cas de perte, sans ouvrir de ticket. Application par role, periode de grace configurable, et deconnexion qui ferme proprement les sessions actives.

5. Detection et incidents : un moteur en temps reel regroupe les evenements bruts en six patterns d’attaque : force brute, credential stuffing, scan distribue, activite post-compromission, cascade de verrouillages et abus protocolaires. Chaque incident dispose d’une vue detaillee : chronologie, IPs sources, comptes cibles, severite, empreinte user-agent et actions de resolution en un clic (reinitialisation de mot de passe, blocage de sous-reseau, marquage resolu).

6. Journal d’activite : piste d’audit conforme des actions admin : installations d’extensions, modifications de reglages, changements de role, creations d’utilisateurs, publications de contenu, changements de theme, evenements 2FA. Filtrage, recherche et export CSV avec retention configurable. Sept domaines de loggers, activables independamment.

7. En-tetes de securite de la page de connexion : Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy et X-Content-Type-Options sur wp-login.php et la page de verrouillage. Deux presets (standard et strict) avec une option de CSP report-uri.

8. Detection de fuites : repere les utilisateurs qui se connectent avec un mot de passe present dans des fuites publiques, via des recherches preservant la vie privee (k-anonymat) sur Have I Been Pwned. Seuls les 5 premiers caracteres hexa d’un prefixe SHA-1 quittent votre serveur ; le mot de passe et le hachage complet ne sortent jamais. Verification e-mail optionnelle (opt-in, desactivee par defaut) via XposedOrNot. Fail-soft : une coupure de HIBP ne bloque jamais la connexion.

En plus

  • Notifications par e-mail, Slack, Discord ou webhook generique, avec validation d’URL anti-SSRF integree, seuil de severite et rate limiting.
  • Suite WP-CLI complete : wp login-armor reset-slug, unblock, whitelist, incidents resolve, purge-logs, 2fa reset, 2fa devices, hardening blacklist. Operations scriptees et recuperation d’urgence depuis la ligne de commande.
  • Widget Tableau de bord : statut de protection en un coup d’oeil depuis n’importe quelle page admin, avec sparkline 14 jours et six metriques cles.

Concu par

Login Armor est concu et maintenu par WPFormation, une agence WordPress francaise obsedee par les sites propres, rapides et audit-ready. On utilise ce plugin sur chaque site qu’on livre.

  • Presentation et roadmap du plugin
  • Guides securite WordPress sur WPFormation

GPL pour toujours. PHP 8.1+. WordPress 6.8+. Zero dependance.

External Services

Webhook Notifications (optional)

When explicitly enabled and configured by the administrator in LoginArmor > Settings > Notifications, the plugin sends incident data to third-party services via webhooks.

Data sent: incident type, severity level, IP address, target username, event count, and site URL.

No data is sent unless the administrator actively enables and configures a notification channel.

  • Slack – Terms of Service | Privacy Policy
  • Discord – Terms of Service | Privacy Policy
  • Custom Webhook URL – User-configured endpoint (administrator’s responsibility)

Gravatar (Automattic)

The Activity Log tab uses WordPress core’s get_avatar() function to display user avatars. WordPress may send a hashed email address to Gravatar servers to retrieve avatar images. This is controlled by Settings > Discussion > Avatars.

  • Gravatar – Automattic Terms of Service | Privacy Policy

Breach Check – Have I Been Pwned (optional)

When the administrator explicitly enables the Breach Check module (LoginArmor > Settings > Breach Check), LoginArmor queries the public Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords API on each successful login and on password changes to detect user passwords that appear in public data breach corpora.

Data sent: the first 5 hex characters of a SHA-1 hash of the password (k-anonymity lookup). The full password and its full hash never leave the server. The API cannot determine which password is being checked – it only sees a 5-character prefix that is mathematically shared with ~500-900 other candidate hashes.

No API key or account is required. The endpoint is free and public.

  • Have I Been Pwned – Pwned Passwords privacy statement | Acceptable Use Policy

Breach Check – XposedOrNot (optional email sub-toggle)

When the administrator additionally enables the Email check sub-toggle inside the Breach Check module (off by default), LoginArmor queries the public XposedOrNot check-email API on new user creation and on email change to detect email addresses that appear in publicly disclosed data breaches.

Data sent: the user’s email address (URL-encoded) and a plugin-identifying User-Agent string. This is unavoidable for the lookup – there is no k-anonymity variant for email breach checks. Because this call transmits an email address to a third party, it is opt-in and off by default.

No API key or account is required. The endpoint is free and public.

  • XposedOrNot – xposedornot.com | Privacy Policy
sections.installation:
1. Upload the login-armor directory to /wp-content/plugins/
  2. Activate the plugin through the ‘Plugins’ menu in WordPress
  3. Go to LoginArmor in the admin menu to configure

For multisite: Network Activate the plugin to apply it across all sites.

Setting up Hide Login

  1. Go to LoginArmor > Settings > Hide Login section
  2. Enter your desired login slug (e.g., my-login)
  3. Save settings
  4. Bookmark your new login URL: you will need it to access your admin

Recovering access

If you forget your custom login URL:

  • Use the recovery email feature (configurable in settings)
  • Connect to your database and delete the login_armor_hide_slug row from the wp_options table
  • Use WP-CLI: wp option delete login_armor_hide_slug
sections.faq:
Will it lock me out of my own site?

No. Hide Login always sends a one-time recovery URL to the admin email. If you lose the slug, check your inbox. The plugin also honors wp-cli fallback so you can reset anything from SSH.

Does it slow my site down?

No. Everything is lazy-loaded and indexed. On a normal login flow the extra SQL cost is under 2 ms.

Is it compatible with Cloudflare / reverse proxies?

Yes. IP detection honors trusted X-Forwarded-For headers; you pick the header in Settings.

Does it work with multisite?

Yes, subdomain and subfolder. Each site has its own modules, logs, and thresholds.

Can I use LoginArmor alongside Wordfence / iThemes Security / Solid Security?

Yes, but disable overlapping modules on one side to avoid double lockouts.

Where is the data stored?

Three custom tables in your own database: events, incidents, activity. Nothing leaves your server.

How do I migrate my configuration?

Settings are plain WordPress options. Export/import via WP-CLI or any standard options-sync tool.

Is there a pro version?

Not currently. LoginArmor is fully free and open source. GPL forever.

Where can I report bugs or request features?

Support forum: wordpress.org/support/plugin/login-armor/.
sections.changelog:
2.0.3

Same-day hotfix on top of 2.0.2. The 2.0.2 fix (clear parent output buffers before writing the body) was correct under HTTP/1.1 — curl tests passed cleanly with 429 + Content-Length + branded body — but Firefox and Chromium on HTTP/2 still hung on “Loading…” because of a separate problem: on LiteSpeed (LSAPI / o2switch PowerBoost), calling fastcgi_finish_request() after a custom 4xx response with a non-default body fails to terminate HTTP/2 streams cleanly. The DATA frames never get an END_STREAM flag, the browser keeps waiting forever for more data.

  • Fix – LoginArmor::flush_response_and_exit() no longer calls fastcgi_finish_request(). It now mirrors WordPress core’s _default_wp_die_handler pattern exactly: discard parent output buffers, set Content-Length, echo body, flush(), exit. The natural SAPI shutdown triggered by exit is what closes the HTTP/2 stream cleanly on LiteSpeed. Verified live on cours-ndrc.fr with Playwright Firefox (gecko 128) — HTTP/2 lockout response now arrives complete in 1.3 seconds instead of timing out at 30+. Same helper is used by the lockout page (LockoutPage), Hide Login’s 404 template renderer, and Hardening’s XML-RPC + access-denied responses, so all four early-exit paths inherit the fix.

2.0.2

Critical fix for the lockout 429 page. The 2.0.1 attempt did not actually deliver the branded page to the client when the lockout was triggered from inside wp_login_failed.

  • Fix – The branded 429 lockout page now actually reaches the browser when the lockout is triggered (attempt #N). Root cause: PHP’s default output buffer (auto-opened by output_buffering=4096 in php.ini, which is the default on most managed hosts) was capturing the page body. fastcgi_finish_request() flushes the FastCGI request to nginx but does NOT flush user-level output buffers, so the body was discarded at PHP shutdown after the FastCGI connection had already been closed. The client received whatever wp-login.php had buffered earlier (the regular login form) instead. Fix: discard every parent output buffer before writing the response in LoginArmor::flush_response_and_exit(). This shared helper is also used by Hide Login’s 404 template renderer and Hardening’s XML-RPC + access-denied responses, so they all benefit from the same fix.

2.0.1

Post-launch patch. Issues caught on the first day on WordPress.org.

  • Fix – The branded 429 lockout landing page is now rendered on the very request that triggers the lockout (attempt #N), not on the next one. Previously a user who reached the lockout threshold still saw the wp-login form with “wrong password” until they clicked submit a second time, which contradicted the readme promise of “locked attackers see a branded 429 landing page”. Achieved by introducing a new action login_armor_lockout_triggered that fires after the lockout marker is committed; LockoutPage subscribes to it and renders + exits inline. The pre-existing login_armor_before_lockout hook is preserved unchanged for back-compat with third-party subscribers.
  • Feature – Two new “Reset” buttons in Settings. “Reset all events & incidents” (Detection & Logs section) wipes the events feed, brute-force counters, and every active or resolved incident in one click; all currently locked-out IPs are immediately released. “Reset all activity entries” (Activity Log section) wipes the admin-action audit trail. Both are confirmation-gated. Distinct from the existing “Purge old logs now” buttons, which only delete rows past their retention threshold.
  • Assets – WordPress.org banner and icon replaced with the navy-blue / yellow-padlock variant that matches the in-admin icon and the rest of the brand identity. The orange variant that shipped with 2.0.0 was an unvalidated draft.

2.0.0

First WordPress.org public release of the V2 line. Bundles every
feature shipped privately as 2.1.x – two-factor authentication
(TOTP + email OTP + backup codes + trusted devices + recovery flow),
Hide Login with a branded 429 lockout landing page, password and
email breach detection, login-page security headers, login-page
hardening (honeypot, reserved-username blacklist), expanded admin
hardening toggles, audit log for admin actions, and a complete WP-CLI
command suite.

Compared to the internal 2.1.5 build, this release adds a final
pre-release security audit pass:

  • Security – Breach Check email lookup is now opt-in by default. The
    password lookup (which transmits only a hashed prefix, no PII) is
    enabled when the module is activated; the email lookup, which
    transmits real email addresses to XposedOrNot, requires explicit
    admin opt-in via the settings form.
  • Security – Reserved-username blacklist now folds via Unicode-to-ASCII
    transliteration before comparison, so homoglyphs (ɑdmin, Ådmin,
    enclosed alphanumerics) collapse onto the same blacklist entry.
  • Security – REST API gating for unauthenticated users now matches
    public namespaces (oembed/, contact-form-7/, wp-site-health/)
    by route prefix on the parsed REST path. The previous substring
    match could be bypassed with a query-string trick.
  • Security – Hide WordPress version toggle now also strips the
    ?ver=X.Y.Z query argument from <script src> and stylesheet
    URLs at script_loader_src priority 9999.
  • Security – .htaccess writes (Block PHP in uploads, Disable
    directory listing) are now atomic via temp file + rename. A failed
    flush surfaces an admin notice instead of leaving the toggle UI out
    of sync with the on-disk state.
  • CLI – The wp login-armor status count of active incidents is now
    prepared via $wpdb->prepare() for discipline consistency.
  • Docs – Login Page Security Headers strict mode docblock rewritten
    to describe the actual tightening (default-src, font-src,
    connect-src boundaries) instead of an inline-script claim that
    never shipped.

2.1.5

  • Fix – CRITICAL: Hide Login regression introduced in 2.1.4. After the WP.org-review cherry-pick, HideLogin::serve_404_template() only flipped $pagenow = 'index.php' and returned, without exiting. But wp-login.php bootstraps itself via wp-load.php (not wp-blog-header.php), so the wp_loaded hook fires inside wp-login.php – without an explicit exit, wp-login.php continued its normal execution and rendered the login form at /wp-login.php. Hide Login was effectively disabled on the /wp-login.php path (the custom slug still worked, but the whole point is to hide /wp-login.php). Fix: render the 404 via get_query_template( '404' ) – theme-only lookup, no direct require of wp-includes/template-loader.php – then exit. Discovered during post-release validation 2026-04-23.

2.1.4

  • Fix – 2FA email delivery failures are now surfaced to the user. Previously, EmailOTP::send_code() could fail silently (SMTP misconfiguration, mail-provider rate limit, wp_mail hook returning false) because the three callers – setup AJAX, intercept_login, and the verification-screen resend – discarded the return value. The setup AJAX now returns an error with an actionable message; the login flow stores a flag on the verification token so the verify screen tells the user that code delivery failed and suggests clicking Resend or contacting the site administrator. Reported by beta tester 2026-04-23.
  • Security – Admin views now pass every inline SVG icon through wp_kses() with an explicit allowlist. A new LoginArmor\Icons::render() helper wraps the previous echo Icons::get( … ) pattern (19 call sites across admin/views/), which let us drop the phpcs:ignore WordPress.Security.EscapeOutput.OutputNotEscaped comments WP.org review flagged on V1. The four remaining printf()-with-phpcs:ignore calls in activity.php, events.php, incidents.php, and overview.php were replaced with echo wp_kses_post( sprintf( … ) ) for the same reason.
  • Build – build-release.sh PRUNE list now drops the root-level assets/ and .wordpress-org/ directories from the release ZIP (WordPress.org directory banners/icons ship via SVN, not inside the plugin). The plugin’s runtime logo was moved from assets/icon-128x128.png to admin/assets/img/icon-128x128.png so the topbar continues to render after the PRUNE. Cherry-picked from V1.0.1 hygiene work.
  • Fix – includes/Notifications/Channels/DiscordChannel.php namespace had a literal space (Login Armor\…) that parse-errored whenever the Discord channel autoloaded. Collapsed to LoginArmor to match the three other notification channels. Cherry-picked from V1.0.1.
  • Fix – HideLogin::serve_404_template() no longer directly requires wp-includes/template-loader.php nor calls wp() manually – both were redundant with WordPress’s wp-blog-header.php request lifecycle. Cherry-picked from V1.0.1.

2.1.3

  • Fix – CRITICAL: the “Disable file editor” toggle in Hardening settings had no effect. The module was registering the file_edit_allowed filter, which does not exist in WordPress core (core only honours the DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT constant, evaluated in map_meta_cap()). Replaced with define('DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true) plus a belt-and-suspenders map_meta_cap filter that force-denies edit_themes, edit_plugins, and edit_files in Hardening::register_disable_file_editor(). Theme File Editor and Plugin File Editor are now correctly blocked when the toggle is on. Reported by beta tester 2026-04-20.
  • Fix – 2FA setup: the “Complete setup” button on the user profile could fail silently. The JS handler had no .catch() and no branch for json.success === false, so if the AJAX request failed (nonce expiration, PHP warning, network hiccup) the page did not reload, the user assumed 2FA was active, but login_armor_2fa_enabled user meta was never written – leaving the account password-only on next login. Aligned the handler on the same .then()/.catch() pattern as “Verify setup”, added an inline error message in the backup-codes step, added the completeFailed localised string. Reported by beta tester 2026-04-20.
  • Fix – 2FA setup: ajax_verify_2fa_setup() used to write login_armor_2fa_confirmed = false while the wizard was waiting on the “I’ve saved my codes” checkbox. WordPress stores a boolean false as an empty string in user meta, creating an ambiguous ghost row. Replaced with delete_user_meta() so the flag simply does not exist until ajax_complete_2fa_setup() writes it to true.
  • Fix – 2FA + Hide Login: HideLogin::get_login_url() returned the custom slug URL even when Hide Login was disabled, as long as a slug remained in the database from a previous configuration. TwoFactor::intercept_login() then redirected to /slug/?login-armor-2fa=verify&token=… – a URL that 404s because Hide Login’s slug routing is inactive. The verification screen was never rendered and the user was stuck on a front-end 404. get_login_url() now returns wp_login_url() unless both a slug is stored AND login_armor_hide_enabled is on. Discovered during pre-release testing 2026-04-20.
  • Fix – 2FA email OTP: the 60-second cooldown was blocking the login flow too, not just the “Resend code” button. After a successful 2FA login, if the user logged out and logged back in within 60 seconds (reasonable during admin work), EmailOTP::send_code() refused to issue a new code, the verification screen rendered without a new email being sent, and the user was stuck. The cooldown now refuses only when a valid un-consumed code is still pending; once the previous code has been validated (transient deleted) or expired, a fresh login flow issues a new code immediately. Discovered during pre-release testing 2026-04-20.
  • Enhancement – wp login-armor 2fa status now shows two additional columns – confirmed and grace_until – and accepts --user=<login|email> to limit the output to a single user. The command no longer errors out when the 2FA module is globally off (it prints a warning and shows the per-user state anyway), which is exactly what you need when diagnosing an incomplete enrollment.

2.1.2

  • Fix – CRITICAL: Branded lockout page now finalises the HTTP/2 stream deterministically. Under LiteSpeed/LSAPI on hosts like o2switch, the 2.1.0/2.1.1 render() → echo → exit() path hung Firefox and Chrome indefinitely (“Loading…” spinner, no response) because the HTTP/2 stream closed without an explicit Content-Length or a fastcgi_finish_request() call. Reproducible on Firefox + cours-ndrc.fr from the 5th failed attempt on a locked IP. Fix: buffer the document with ob_start(), emit Content-Length, then fastcgi_finish_request() (fallback: ob_end_flush() + flush()). HTTP/1.1 clients were unaffected, which is why the bug slipped through the 2.1.0 deep audit on WordPress Playground (Playground uses a different PHP runtime).

2.1.1

  • Fix – Branded lockout page: is_login_url_request() is now case-insensitive (stripos + strcasecmp). Hosts that serve /WP-LOGIN.PHP (Windows IIS, Apache rewrites with [NC]) were bypassing the branded takeover and falling back to the stock WP form. Found during the v2.1.0 deep audit on WordPress Playground (2026-04-20).
  • Security – Branded lockout page now emits X-Frame-Options: DENY to deny any framing attempt. No interactive CTA on the page so clickjacking impact was low, but the header aligns the response with class-login-headers.php for consistency.
  • Security – Defense-in-depth: the --la-accent CSS custom property in the branded page is now passed through esc_attr(). Currently hardcoded so no user input reaches it, but a future filter surface would have been an XSS vector without escaping.
  • Fix – uninstall.php now clears the login_armor_cleanup_rate_key single event alongside the other cron hooks. Previous behaviour left one ephemeral cron entry for up to one hour after uninstall – functionally harmless (it self-purges at fire time because the target option is gone) but visible in wp_cron().
  • Fix – Inline output escaping in LockoutPage::render(). Plugin Check flagged six EscapeOutput.OutputNotEscaped errors because the heading, body, and locale strings were pre-escaped into intermediate variables and echoed directly; PHPCS does not follow data flow. Every echo now inlines its own esc_html_e() / esc_attr() call. Values were already escaped, so no runtime behaviour change – the refactor only satisfies the Plugin Check bar WP.org enforces.

2.1.0

  • New – Branded lockout landing page on the login URL for locked IPs. Niveau 1 (20 min) returns HTTP 429 with a live countdown; Niveau 2 blacklist returns HTTP 403 with a “contact administrator” message. Self-contained HTML with inline CSS + vanilla JS countdown, emits Cache-Control: no-store so WP Rocket / LiteSpeed / W3TC never cache the per-IP response. Class LoginArmor\Lockout\LockoutPage at plugins_loaded priority 9998 (one tick before Hide Login). Subnet-blocked IPs also land on the branded page (rendered as Niveau 2).
  • Change – Incidents UI copy aligned with actual scope: pill “IP blocked” becomes “Auth blocked”, new “Blacklist 24h” pill for re-lockouts within 24 h, timeline event reason and Events sidebar legend follow the same rename. The plugin gates authentication, not the whole IP – the label now says so honestly. Status badge BLOCKED unchanged (severity category, not a scope label).
  • Fix – LOGIN_ARMOR_VERSION constant was stuck at 2.0.8 since v2.0.9 shipped (only the plugin header was bumped, the constant was missed). Now tracks 2.1.0.
  • i18n – Regenerated login-armor.pot from current source, added FR translations for the 7 new v2.1 strings (all locked verbatim by design review, no em dash per project convention), removed 6 orphan msgids that were no longer referenced in PHP, and compiled a fresh login-armor-fr_FR.mo.

2.0.9

  • Security – Brute-force lockout now extends beyond the login form. Once an IP is locked, the same window also rejects lost-password submissions (no more reset-email flooding), password-reset email delivery (retrieve_password_notification_email), reset-link validation (allow_password_reset), user registration (registration_errors), XML-RPC (xmlrpc_enabled, neutralises system.multicall credential-stuffing amplifiers), and REST enumeration on /wp-json/wp/v2/users (rest_authentication_errors). Six new hooks in includes/class-limit-login.php, no DB schema change. The pre-existing 2-tier short/long ban mechanism is preserved (defaults rebalanced to 2 lockouts in 24 h → 24 h ban).
  • Fix – Events tab: IPv6 addresses no longer overflow the Source IP column. The column is widened from 150 to 190-200 px and .la-evt-ip / .la-live-events__ip now wrap with overflow-wrap: anywhere + word-break: break-all so long IPv6 (e.g. 2001:67c:289c:4::131) stays inside its cell instead of bleeding into “User · action”. Same fix applied to the Overview live-events widget. Reported by beta tester 2026-04-19.
  • Fix – Events tab: attempts made against an already-locked IP are now correctly classified as locked instead of failed in wp_login_armor_logs, removing the misleading “Mot de passe incorrect” entries that appeared after “Débit limité” rows for the same IP. Belt-and-suspenders fix on top of the existing 2.0.3 double-log dedup: log_failure() now queries LimitLogin::is_ip_locked() and disambiguates the triggering attempt (real password failure) from post-lockout attempts via a request-scoped lockout_just_triggered flag. Reported by beta tester 2026-04-19.
  • Note – Branded landing page on the login URL for locked IPs and the “Auth bloquée” / “Blacklist 24h” Incidents pill rename are deferred to v2.1.

2.0.8

  • Fix – Hide Login: the “Lost your password?” form submission now lands on the confirmation screen instead of a 404. WordPress core’s wp_safe_redirect() resolves the relative target wp-login.php?checkemail=confirm against the spoofed REQUEST_URI (/<slug>/?action=lostpassword) before our wp_redirect filter sees it, producing /<slug>/wp-login.php?.... Naive substring replacement then doubled the slug to /<slug>/<slug>/?.... The rewriter now collapses the duplicated slug segment back to a single one. The reset email itself was always sent – only the post-submit confirmation page was unreachable. (2.0.7 attempted this fix but only handled the bare relative form, which WP core never actually emits to the filter.)

2.0.7

  • Fix – Hide Login: first attempt at the lostpassword 404 fix above. Insufficient – only handled the bare relative URL form; in practice WP core resolves the relative URL via REQUEST_URI before our filter runs. Superseded by 2.0.8 on the same day.

2.0.6

  • Fix – Overview hero: stray em dash rendered when no login event had been recorded yet (“System last checked -.”). The “last checked” clause is now omitted entirely in that state and a dedicated copy is shown instead. Stale bytecode on hosts with opcache.validate_timestamps=0 is also handled via a defensive trim at the template level.
  • New – Overview hero: 4th metric “Data breach” shown when Breach Check is enabled. Highlights in amber when at least one account is flagged, so the hero no longer announces “Your site is fully defended” without surfacing the outstanding leak.
  • Fix – Breach Check top banner on Overview was hidden in practice: the $la_breach_on / $la_breach_flagged variables were defined below the hero block instead of above it, so the conditional always evaluated falsy. Hoisted the Breach Check state to the top of the template.
  • Fix – Plugin activation now walks every PHP file and calls opcache_invalidate() so hosts that disable timestamp validation pick up new bytecode without needing a PHP-FPM restart.

2.0.5

  • New – Breach Check module (opt-in). Quietly compares each login password against the Have I Been Pwned public corpus using the privacy-preserving k-anonymity range API – only the first 5 characters of a SHA-1 hash ever leave your server. A matching user gets a factual, non-alarmist notice on their own profile page inviting them to change the password. Admins see the flagged count on Overview and on the dashboard widget. Optionally also checks email addresses against the XposedOrNot public breach list on user creation and email change (off by default, separate sub-toggle). Zero dependencies installed, no API key, no account – both backing services are free public endpoints. Fail-soft (3 s timeout, any error silently aborts the check), cached 24 h per input, never blocks a login. An optional “force password reset” setting nags flagged users to change the password by redirecting them to their profile – the account is never locked out.
  • Changed – Security score weights rebalanced: Hide Login and Brute Force drop from 20 back to 15 pts each (had been temporarily bumped in 2.0.4 after Salt Rotation was removed), Breach Check adds 10 pts. Sites that hit 100 on 2.0.4 will drop to 90 until Breach Check is enabled – a deliberate nudge toward the new module.
  • UX – Protection-modules grid fills its 8th slot again. The Overview bento and the dashboard widget no longer show a visible empty cell (7-in-8 grid) that 2.0.4 introduced when Salt Rotation was removed.
  • Security – All new code path reviewed for SSRF, timing, XSS, CSRF, rate-limit, privacy and self-lockout. URLs are hardcoded, only a 5-char hex prefix or a URL-encoded email is appended; suffix comparison uses hash_equals() for constant-time matching; all AJAX endpoints pass through the existing nonce + capability guard; user-meta outputs are esc_html()‘d; the module cannot return a WP_Error from the authenticate filter.

2.0.4

  • Removed – Salt Keys Rotation module. The feature required wp-config.php to be writable by the web user, which is not the case on most managed WordPress hosts (file permanently set to 444). Presenting a feature the typical user cannot activate was confusing; the module has been removed from the Settings tab, Overview protection cards, dashboard widget, security-score calculation and WP-CLI. The 10 points that Salt Rotation contributed to the score were redistributed between Hide Login (+5) and Brute Force (+5) so scores top out at 100 as before. If you still need to rotate your salts, regenerate them manually at https://api.wordpress.org/secret-key/1.1/salt/ and paste them into wp-config.php over SSH/SFTP.
  • Fix – Incidents: 5 real failed attempts were counted as 10 events on each incident, because one attempt past the lockout threshold was logged twice (once as locked by log_blocked(), once as failed by log_failure() since 2.0.3 removed the lockout guard to preserve the lockout-triggering attempt). The second log is now suppressed by a request-scoped flag, so one blocked attempt produces exactly one row.
  • Fix – Incidents: 5 attempts on a nonexistent user created two open incidents (BRUTE_FORCE + ENUMERATION) instead of one. check_enumeration() now skips when check_brute_force() or check_credential_stuffing() would match the same metrics snapshot, and check_brute_force() auto-resolves any still-active ENUMERATION incident on the same IP and inherits its started_at so the window reflects the full attack, not just the threshold-crossing moment.
  • UX – Hide Login: a pre-activation modal lets you choose your secret login URL (with a random suggestion, a Regenerate button, and an opt-in recovery email) before the module is activated. The old forced post-activation reminder modal is removed.
  • UX – Incidents: every incident card and drill-down now shows an amber “IP locked” pill with remaining minutes when the attacker IP is under an active lockout, and a red “Subnet blocked” pill with the /24 CIDR when that IP falls inside a manually-blocklisted subnet. The pills sit directly under the source IP in the card header. The action row swaps Block subnet for “Remove from blocklist” when appropriate and adds an “Unblock IP” button when the IP is locked – no more opening the drill-down to discover state or unblock.
  • UX – Overview: protection-module cards no longer show an underline on their title/subtitle when you hover over a tile, and the “Investigate” CTA on incident cards no longer shows one either. Both were leaking through WordPress admin’s global a:hover { text-decoration: underline } rule.
  • Refactor – ajax_regenerate_slug no longer auto-sends a recovery email; email delivery is an explicit opt-in action.
  • Internal – LimitLogin::get_block_status( $ip ) helper + new AJAX endpoint login_armor_subnet_unblock.

2.0.3

  • Hotfix – Overview: fixed a reload loop that triggered on fresh installs (zero logged events). A stale JS selector looking for the old Lot 17 .la-allquiet card kept firing window.location.reload() on every 10 s poll once the backend reported the all-quiet state. The JS now reads the hero’s data-la-allquiet attribute and only reloads when the quiet state truly flips. Reported on a first-time activation.
  • Fix – Incidents timeline: IPv6 addresses (~39 chars) no longer overflow the grid column and overlap the username / reason column. Fixed-width IP column replaced by auto sizing so IPv4 stays compact and IPv6 gets the room it needs.
  • Fix – Settings · Hardening: the outer “X of 13” counter on the module summary now updates live when toggles are flipped, and correctly reflects the saved state after the save-all AJAX. Previously it stayed stuck at its server-rendered value until a full page reload.
  • Fix – Detection: the failed login attempt that triggers the lockout is no longer silently dropped from the events log. The Events tab now shows the full chronology (all failed attempts + subsequent locked attempts) and the attack-pattern classifier sees the correct total.
  • Fix – Confirmation modals: the “I understand” checkbox label is now correctly translated in every admin modal (was falling back to English everywhere except on the 2FA profile page). Root cause: the JS captured the i18n strings at IIFE load time, before admin.js’ wp_localize_script had produced the window.loginArmor global. The check-label strings are now read lazily at modal open time.
  • Fix – Confirmation modals: the “I understand” checkbox no longer shows on modals that did not request it (unblock IP, block subnet, etc.). A base CSS rule display:flex on the checkbox wrapper was overriding the HTML hidden attribute – added [hidden] selector to honor it.
  • Security – Hide Login: the default slug on first activation is now a cryptographically random 8-char string instead of the literal "loginarmor" which any scanner that detected the plugin would trivially try first. Merely opening the Settings tab no longer writes this public string to the database either – it stays a display-only placeholder for the URL preview, persisted to the DB only when the user actually activates the module (at which point the random slug is written). Installations that had been auto-stamped with login_armor_hide_slug = "loginarmor" but never enabled Hide Login will get a fresh random slug on the next enable.

2.0.2

  • Hotfix – Hide Login: fixed a regression where the admin password-reset email link landed on “invalid key” with no reset form rendered. Caused by the password-reset cookie being scoped to /wp-login.php instead of the custom slug, so the browser did not send it back on the post-click redirect. Admin password recovery now works end-to-end on all Hide Login configurations. Reported by Sébastien Pierrepack.

2.0.1

  • i18n: Full French translation (907 strings after the code-i18n refactor), strict WordPress FR Polyglots compliance (glossary, epicene writing, curly apostrophes, non-breaking spaces, accented capitals).
  • i18n: load_plugin_textdomain() now loads the bundled .mo on local / non-wp.org installs – previously the French catalog was ignored on dev.
  • i18n: Widget dashboard, Activity log (CHANGED/UPDATED/ROTATED badges, USER/POST/PLUGIN object labels, time-ago cells), Events log, Incidents drill-down timeline (6h ago → il y a 6h, Apr 18 → avr 18) and Overview last-check sentence all translate on fr_FR sites.
  • i18n: WordPress role names (Administrator, Editor, …) in the 2FA Enforcement checkboxes and Activity role cell now use WP core’s translate_user_role() helper.
  • i18n: admin.js live-events polling and brute-force summary template localized via wp_localize_script().
  • i18n: Bundled languages/login-armor-fr_FR.po|mo (98 KB) so the plugin ships fully translated on French WordPress installs.
  • readme: Bilingual rewrite (English first, French after) with a commercial angle covering all nine v2 modules.
  • build: scripts/i18n/compile-mo.php fixed to emit proper gettext plural encoding (was silently dropping 13 plural forms).

2.0.0

  • New: Two-Factor Authentication module – TOTP (authenticator apps), Email OTP, and backup codes, with per-role enforcement and configurable grace periods
  • New: standalone 2FA verification screen integrated with the Hide Login custom slug
  • New: per-user 2FA section in the WordPress profile page with setup wizard, QR code generator, and backup code download
  • New: WP-CLI command wp login-armor 2fa status|reset
  • New: activity log events for 2FA (enabled, disabled, verified, failed, backup used)
  • New: dashboard overview bento card and dashboard widget module for 2FA
  • Security: per-IP rate limiting on 2FA verification (sliding window, 10 failures per 15 minutes)
  • Security: wp_validate_redirect() on the post-login redirect_to parameter
  • Security: audit-trail hook fired on TOTP decryption failures (useful after AUTH_KEY rotation)
  • Accessibility: aria-label and aria-describedby on 2FA code inputs
  • Fix: login form action preserved trailing slash to prevent POST → GET conversion behind some web servers
  • Fix: Hide Login URL preserved trailing slash to prevent POST → GET conversion during login
  • Fix: QR code generator rewritten in client-side JS for reliable scanning across authenticator apps
  • Fix: 2FA setup wizard now advances correctly to the backup codes step after TOTP verification
  • Fix: 2FA verify handler now binds to every wizard step and reads the active step input
  • UX: calm “All quiet” hero on the Overview when the site has been silent for 24 hours, with a single proactive advice CTA (Lot 17)
  • UX: unified confirmation modal replacing every window.confirm() in the admin – keyboard accessible, focus-trapped, variants for danger/primary actions (Lot 17)
  • UX: Salt Rotator “Rotate now” modal now detects and surfaces the backup age; sticky banner reminds admins of the first scheduled rotation until it lands (Lot 15)
  • Hardening: new toggle to block reserved usernames at login and registration (Lot 14)
  • Hardening: new toggle for an anti-bot honeypot on login/register/lostpassword forms (Lot 14)
  • 2FA: trusted devices – after a successful verification, optionally trust the current browser for 7 to 90 days so subsequent logins skip the 2FA challenge. Auto-revoked on password reset, 2FA disable, and AUTH_KEY rotation (Lot 16)
  • 2FA: account recovery – when every 2FA method is lost, the user can request a reset; a signed single-use link is emailed to the first site administrator who authorizes the operation (Lot 16)
  • WP-CLI: wp login-armor 2fa devices list|revoke (Lot 16)
  • UI: pixel-perfect admin redesign – self-hosted Inter + JetBrains Mono fonts, new navy hero with 104px count-up, animated 24h activity chart, 8-card protection modules grid, sticky events table with streaming pill, Settings screen with weighted 0-100 security score ring (Lot 18)
  • UI: central Lucide-style icon helper LoginArmor\Icons and new tokens.css scoped under body.login-armor-page – zero external CDN (Lot 18)

1.0.0

  • Initial release
  • Hide Login: custom login URL slug with configurable redirect and recovery email
  • Brute Force Protection: lockout escalation, subnet blocking, IP safelist
  • Hardening: 10 security toggles with recommended defaults button
  • Detection Engine: 5 attack patterns with automatic classification
  • Incidents Dashboard: severity levels, drill-down investigation, resolve/ignore
  • Events Log: paginated login attempts with filters and CSV export
  • Activity Log: 30 events across 6 domains (Users, Posts, Media, Plugins, Themes, Options)
  • Notifications: Email, Slack, Discord, and custom webhook channels
  • WP-CLI: 8 commands for full command-line management
  • Dashboard Widget: security status overview on the WP Dashboard
  • Multisite support with network activation

short_description: Eight security modules in one lightweight plugin: hide login, brute force lockout, 2FA, audit log, hardening. No bloat, no upsells, GPL.
description:
Eight security layers. One lightweight plugin. Zero compromise.

Login Armor is a complete WordPress security stack built for agencies, freelancers and pros who deliver audit-ready sites. No premium tier, no bundled marketing dashboard, no telemetry. Every module runs locally, ships with safe defaults, and stays out of your way.

Stop juggling Wordfence’s bloat, Solid Security’s upsells, and Limit Login Attempts’ gaps. Login Armor delivers eight independent modules in under one megabyte, with the discipline of an enterprise plugin and the licensing of free software.

Why Login Armor

  • No upsells, ever. No “premium” tier, no “Pro” buttons greyed out in your admin. Every feature is GPL.
  • No external services to sign up for. No API keys, no remote dashboards, no third-party telemetry. Two optional integrations (Have I Been Pwned for breach detection, Slack/Discord/webhook for notifications) only fire when you explicitly enable them.
  • Built to be invisible. Sub-megabyte ZIP, lazy-loaded modules, indexed queries. The plugin’s footprint stays under 2 ms on a normal login flow.
  • Multisite-aware, PHP 8.1-native. Network-activate on a fleet, configure per-site, manage from the shell with a complete WP-CLI command suite.
  • Production-grade defaults. Every toggle ships with the value an experienced admin would pick anyway. Zero-config gets you 80 percent of the protection.

Eight independent modules

1. Hide Login – Replace wp-login.php with a custom slug. Anyone hitting the old URL gets a 404 from your theme – no leakage that WordPress is even installed. Compatible with multisite, password-protected posts, reverse proxies, and password recovery flows. The branded pre-activation modal lets you pick or generate the slug before flipping the switch, and emails it to you so you can’t lock yourself out.

2. Brute Force Protection – Cascading lockouts after repeated failed logins. Locked attackers see a branded 429 landing page with a live countdown. Repeated lockouts escalate to a 24-hour ban. Lostpassword, register, XML-RPC and the REST users endpoint are all gated when an IP is locked, so attackers can’t pivot. Subnet blocking handles distributed attacks. Trusted X-Forwarded-For for sites behind Cloudflare or a load balancer.

3. Hardening – Thirteen one-click toggles across surface reduction, credential hardening, and request filtering. Disable XML-RPC, the theme/plugin file editor, the WordPress version exposure (including ?ver= on assets, even for WP 6.5+ ES modules), application passwords, author enumeration, and more. Block reserved usernames with Unicode-confusable detection. Add an invisible login honeypot. Block PHP execution in uploads and directory listing via atomic-write .htaccess rules.

4. Two-Factor Authentication – Enterprise-grade 2FA in three flavours: TOTP via any authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden), one-time codes by email, and printable backup codes. Trusted devices remembered for thirty days so you only verify once per browser. A recovery flow lets a user reset their second factor by email when the authenticator is lost, without a support ticket. Per-role enforcement, configurable grace period, and a session-aware logout.

5. Detection and Incidents – A real-time detection engine groups raw events into six attack patterns: brute force, credential stuffing, distributed scan, post-compromise activity, lockout cascade, and protocol abuse. Each incident has a drill-down view with timeline, source IPs, target users, severity, user-agent fingerprint, and one-click resolution actions (reset password, block subnet, mark resolved).

6. Activity Log – Compliance-ready audit trail of admin actions: plugin installs, settings changes, role updates, user creation, content publishing, theme switches, 2FA enrollment events. Filter, search and export to CSV with configurable retention. Seven logger domains, all togglable independently.

7. Login Page Security Headers – Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy and X-Content-Type-Options on wp-login.php and the lockout page. Two presets (standard and strict) with an optional CSP report-uri.

8. Breach Check – Detect users logging in with a password that appears in public data breach corpora, using privacy-preserving k-anonymity lookups against Have I Been Pwned. Only the first 5 hex characters of a SHA-1 prefix leave the server, the password and full hash never travel. Optional opt-in email lookup against XposedOrNot. Fail-soft: a HIBP outage never blocks login.

Plus

  • Notifications by email, Slack, Discord, or generic webhook with built-in SSRF-safe URL validation, severity threshold and rate limiting.
  • WP-CLI command suite – wp login-armor reset-slug, unblock, whitelist, incidents resolve, purge-logs, 2fa reset, 2fa devices, hardening blacklist. Full scripted operations and emergency recovery from the shell.
  • Dashboard widget – at-a-glance protection status from any admin page, with a 14-day sparkline and the six headline metrics.

Built by

Login Armor is built and maintained by WPFormation, a French WordPress agency obsessed with sites that are clean, fast, and audit-ready. We use this plugin on every site we ship.

  • Plugin overview and roadmap
  • WordPress security guides on WPFormation

GPL forever. PHP 8.1+. WordPress 6.8+. Zero dependencies.

Huit couches de securite. Un seul plugin leger. Zero compromis.

Login Armor est une stack complete de securite WordPress concue pour les agences, les freelances et les pros qui livrent des sites prets a passer un audit. Pas de version premium, pas de tableau de bord marketing integre, pas de telemetrie. Chaque module tourne en local, embarque des reglages par defaut securises, et reste discret.

Fini de jongler entre la lourdeur de Wordfence, les fenetres d’upsell de Solid Security et les angles morts de Limit Login Attempts. Login Armor regroupe huit modules independants en moins d’un mega-octet, avec la rigueur d’un plugin entreprise et la licence d’un logiciel libre.

Pourquoi Login Armor

  • Aucun upsell, jamais. Pas de niveau “premium”, pas de boutons “Pro” grises dans votre admin. Tout est en GPL.
  • Aucun service externe a activer. Pas de cle API, pas de tableau distant, pas de telemetrie tierce. Les deux integrations optionnelles (Have I Been Pwned pour la detection de fuites, Slack ou Discord ou webhook pour les notifications) ne se declenchent que si vous les activez explicitement.
  • Concu pour etre invisible. ZIP de moins d’un mega, modules charges a la demande, requetes indexees. L’empreinte sur un flux de connexion normal reste sous 2 ms.
  • Compatible multisite, natif PHP 8.1. Activation reseau possible sur une flotte, configuration par site, pilotage depuis la ligne de commande via une suite WP-CLI complete.
  • Reglages par defaut prets pour la production. Chaque bascule arrive avec la valeur qu’un admin experimente choisirait. Sans configuration, vous avez deja 80 % de la protection.

Huit modules independants

1. Masquer la connexion : remplace wp-login.php par une URL personnalisee. Toute tentative sur l’ancienne URL renvoie une 404 du theme, sans reveler la presence de WordPress. Compatible multisite, articles proteges par mot de passe, reverse proxies, et flux de recuperation de mot de passe. La modale de pre-activation vous laisse choisir ou generer le slug avant d’activer le module, et vous l’envoie par e-mail pour eviter tout verrouillage.

2. Protection contre la force brute : verrouillages en cascade apres plusieurs echecs. Les attaquants verrouilles voient une page 429 brandee avec un compte a rebours en direct. Les verrouillages repetes montent a un bannissement de 24 h. Les pages lostpassword, register, XML-RPC et l’endpoint REST users sont egalement bloques pour les IPs verrouillees, pour empecher le pivot. Blocage de sous-reseaux pour les attaques distribuees. Support de X-Forwarded-For pour les sites derriere Cloudflare ou un load balancer.

3. Renforcement : treize bascules en un clic, regroupees en reduction de surface, durcissement des identifiants et filtrage des requetes. Desactivation de XML-RPC, de l’editeur de fichiers theme/extension, de l’exposition de la version WordPress (y compris le ?ver= sur les assets, meme les modules ES de WP 6.5+), des mots de passe applicatifs, de l’enumeration des auteurs. Blocage des identifiants reserves avec detection des homoglyphes Unicode. Pot de miel invisible sur le formulaire de connexion. Blocage de l’execution PHP dans wp-content/uploads/ et desactivation du listing de repertoires via des regles .htaccess ecrites en mode atomique.

4. Authentification a deux facteurs : 2FA prete pour la production avec trois methodes : TOTP via n’importe quelle application authenticator (Google Authenticator, Authy, 1Password, Bitwarden), codes a usage unique par e-mail, codes de secours imprimables. Appareils de confiance memorises pendant trente jours, vous ne validez qu’une fois par navigateur. Une procedure de recuperation laisse l’utilisateur reinitialiser son second facteur par e-mail en cas de perte, sans ouvrir de ticket. Application par role, periode de grace configurable, et deconnexion qui ferme proprement les sessions actives.

5. Detection et incidents : un moteur en temps reel regroupe les evenements bruts en six patterns d’attaque : force brute, credential stuffing, scan distribue, activite post-compromission, cascade de verrouillages et abus protocolaires. Chaque incident dispose d’une vue detaillee : chronologie, IPs sources, comptes cibles, severite, empreinte user-agent et actions de resolution en un clic (reinitialisation de mot de passe, blocage de sous-reseau, marquage resolu).

6. Journal d’activite : piste d’audit conforme des actions admin : installations d’extensions, modifications de reglages, changements de role, creations d’utilisateurs, publications de contenu, changements de theme, evenements 2FA. Filtrage, recherche et export CSV avec retention configurable. Sept domaines de loggers, activables independamment.

7. En-tetes de securite de la page de connexion : Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy et X-Content-Type-Options sur wp-login.php et la page de verrouillage. Deux presets (standard et strict) avec une option de CSP report-uri.

8. Detection de fuites : repere les utilisateurs qui se connectent avec un mot de passe present dans des fuites publiques, via des recherches preservant la vie privee (k-anonymat) sur Have I Been Pwned. Seuls les 5 premiers caracteres hexa d’un prefixe SHA-1 quittent votre serveur ; le mot de passe et le hachage complet ne sortent jamais. Verification e-mail optionnelle (opt-in, desactivee par defaut) via XposedOrNot. Fail-soft : une coupure de HIBP ne bloque jamais la connexion.

En plus

  • Notifications par e-mail, Slack, Discord ou webhook generique, avec validation d’URL anti-SSRF integree, seuil de severite et rate limiting.
  • Suite WP-CLI complete : wp login-armor reset-slug, unblock, whitelist, incidents resolve, purge-logs, 2fa reset, 2fa devices, hardening blacklist. Operations scriptees et recuperation d’urgence depuis la ligne de commande.
  • Widget Tableau de bord : statut de protection en un coup d’oeil depuis n’importe quelle page admin, avec sparkline 14 jours et six metriques cles.

Concu par

Login Armor est concu et maintenu par WPFormation, une agence WordPress francaise obsedee par les sites propres, rapides et audit-ready. On utilise ce plugin sur chaque site qu’on livre.

  • Presentation et roadmap du plugin
  • Guides securite WordPress sur WPFormation

GPL pour toujours. PHP 8.1+. WordPress 6.8+. Zero dependance.

External Services

Webhook Notifications (optional)

When explicitly enabled and configured by the administrator in LoginArmor > Settings > Notifications, the plugin sends incident data to third-party services via webhooks.

Data sent: incident type, severity level, IP address, target username, event count, and site URL.

No data is sent unless the administrator actively enables and configures a notification channel.

  • Slack – Terms of Service | Privacy Policy
  • Discord – Terms of Service | Privacy Policy
  • Custom Webhook URL – User-configured endpoint (administrator’s responsibility)

Gravatar (Automattic)

The Activity Log tab uses WordPress core’s get_avatar() function to display user avatars. WordPress may send a hashed email address to Gravatar servers to retrieve avatar images. This is controlled by Settings > Discussion > Avatars.

  • Gravatar – Automattic Terms of Service | Privacy Policy

Breach Check – Have I Been Pwned (optional)

When the administrator explicitly enables the Breach Check module (LoginArmor > Settings > Breach Check), LoginArmor queries the public Have I Been Pwned Pwned Passwords API on each successful login and on password changes to detect user passwords that appear in public data breach corpora.

Data sent: the first 5 hex characters of a SHA-1 hash of the password (k-anonymity lookup). The full password and its full hash never leave the server. The API cannot determine which password is being checked – it only sees a 5-character prefix that is mathematically shared with ~500-900 other candidate hashes.

No API key or account is required. The endpoint is free and public.

  • Have I Been Pwned – Pwned Passwords privacy statement | Acceptable Use Policy

Breach Check – XposedOrNot (optional email sub-toggle)

When the administrator additionally enables the Email check sub-toggle inside the Breach Check module (off by default), LoginArmor queries the public XposedOrNot check-email API on new user creation and on email change to detect email addresses that appear in publicly disclosed data breaches.

Data sent: the user’s email address (URL-encoded) and a plugin-identifying User-Agent string. This is unavoidable for the lookup – there is no k-anonymity variant for email breach checks. Because this call transmits an email address to a third party, it is opt-in and off by default.

No API key or account is required. The endpoint is free and public.

  • XposedOrNot – xposedornot.com | Privacy Policy

screenshots.caption: Quick tour of all eight modules - Hide Login, Hardening, 2FA setup with QR code, Incidents drill-down, Activity Log, Events, and Overview dashboard.
Overview dashboard - health cards, security pulse, live event tail, threat banner that surfaces active attacks.
Incidents - real-time pattern detection grouped by attack class with severity and one-click resolution.
Incident drill-down - full timeline, user-agent fingerprint, suggested actions, escalation flag.
Events - complete login attempts log with filters and CSV export.
Activity Log - admin action audit trail across seven domains, filterable and exportable.
Settings - modular configuration with live security score and a sticky save bar.
Hide Login pre-activation modal - pick or generate the secret URL and email it to yourself before flipping the switch.
Hardening - thirteen one-click toggles grouped by surface reduction, credential hardening, and request filtering.
Two-factor authentication setup - QR code for any authenticator app, copy-paste fallback, and live verification.
Breach Check - fully transparent k-anonymity lookups, separate password and email toggles, opt-in email check disabled by default.
